title: 22 — Design a Hotel Reservation System
html:
22 — Design a Hotel Reservation System

The one idea: reservations are a concurrency problem, not a scale problem. Model inventory as one row per (hotel, room_type, date) with total and reserved counts, guard updates with a constraint or optimistic lock so two people can't take the last room, and make booking idempotent so a double-click can't book twice.

Step 1 — Scope

  • Hotel chain: 5,000 hotels, 1M rooms.
  • Show hotel/room pages; reserve a room (by room type, not room number); admin add/remove/update rooms; cancel.
  • 10% overbooking allowed.
  • Price can change daily. Payment is full at booking.
  • High concurrency (popular hotels, peak seasons); moderate latency acceptable.

Estimates: 70% occupancy, 3-night stays → ~240,000 reservations/day ≈ 3 reservations/s. Page views at ~10× per funnel step → reservation page ~30 QPS, detail views ~300 QPS. Low QPS — the challenge is correctness.

Step 2 — High-level design

API

GET    /v1/hotels/{id}
GET    /v1/rooms/{id}
POST   /v1/reservations         { hotelId, roomTypeId, startDate, endDate, reservationId }
GET    /v1/reservations/{id}
DELETE /v1/reservations/{id}

reservationId is generated client-side (or fetched first) — it's the idempotency key.

Data model

Relational DB ✅ — read-heavy, ACID guarantees prevent double booking, and the data is clearly relational.

hotel                    (hotel_id, name, address, …)
room_type_rate           (hotel_id, date, room_type_id, rate)
room_type_inventory      (hotel_id, room_type_id, date, total_inventory, total_reserved)   PK(hotel_id, room_type_id, date)
reservation              (reservation_id PK, hotel_id, room_type_id, start_date, end_date, status, guest_id)

Inventory rows are prepopulated for 2 years ahead by a daily job: 5,000 hotels × 20 room types × 730 days ≈ 73M rows — fits one DB (with replicas).

title: Hotel reservation — high-level architecture
---
flowchart LR
    U["User / Admin"] --> CDN["CDN"]
    U --> GW["API gateway"]
    GW --> HS["Hotel service"] --> HDB[("Hotel DB + cache")]
    GW --> RS["Rate service"]
    GW --> RVS["Reservation service"] --> RDB[("Reservation + inventory DB")]
    GW --> PS["Payment service"]
    GW --> HMS["Hotel management service"]

Step 3 — Deep dive

3.1 Checking availability

For each date in the stay:

SELECT date, total_inventory, total_reserved
FROM room_type_inventory
WHERE hotel_id = @h AND room_type_id = @rt AND date BETWEEN @start AND @end;
-- available if total_reserved + @rooms <= 110% × total_inventory for every date

3.2 Concurrency — the heart of the problem

Problem 1: the same user clicks "Book" twice.

  • Client-side: disable the button (not enough on its own).
  • Server-side: idempotent API — reservation_id is the primary key; a second insert with the same key fails with a unique-constraint error and returns the existing reservation.

Problem 2: two users book the last room at the same time. Both read reserved = 99, total = 100, both write 100 → overbooked.

Option How Pros Cons
Pessimistic locking SELECT … FOR UPDATE (SQL Server: UPDLOCK, HOLDLOCK) Simple, correct Lock contention; deadlocks with multi-row ranges; poor scalability
Optimistic locking version column; UPDATE … WHERE version = @v; 0 rows → retry No locks; fast when contention is low ✅ Many retries under high contention
Database constraint CHECK (total_reserved <= total_inventory * 1.1); update and let the DB reject Easy, atomic Constraint logic lives in DB; harder to version; not all DBs support it identically

With ~3 reservations/s, optimistic locking or a constraint is the right call. A single atomic conditional update does both:

UPDATE room_type_inventory
SET total_reserved = total_reserved + @rooms
WHERE hotel_id = @h AND room_type_id = @rt AND date BETWEEN @start AND @end
  AND total_reserved + @rooms <= total_inventory * 1.1;
-- rows affected must equal number of nights, else roll back

3.3 Scaling (if it became a booking.com-sized system)

  • Shard by hotel_id — all queries include it; 16 shards × ~30 QPS is trivial.
  • Inventory cache in Redis for the availability read path (hotel:rt:date → available), with the DB as source of truth for the write; cache updated via CDC. Cache may briefly show a room that's gone — the DB check rejects the booking.

3.4 Data consistency across microservices

If reservation and payment are separate services with separate DBs, a booking spans both. Options: 2PC (blocking, rarely used) or a saga (local transactions + compensating actions: payment fails → release inventory). Pragmatic choice: keep reservation + inventory in one DB so the critical invariant is a single ACID transaction.

Step 4 — Wrap-up

Idempotency key, one ACID transaction for the invariant, optimistic locking for low contention, cache for reads, shard by hotel, sagas where services must be split.

.NET / Azure mapping

  • EF Core optimistic concurrency: a rowversion column mapped with [Timestamp] / .IsRowVersion(); SaveChanges throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException on conflict → retry with fresh data.
  • Or run the conditional UPDATE with Dapper / ExecuteUpdateAsync and check the affected-row count.
  • Idempotency: unique index on ReservationId; catch SqlException 2627/2601 → return the existing booking (201 → 200 with the same body).
  • Azure SQL with CHECK constraints; read replicas for availability search.
  • Sagas: MassTransit state machines or Durable Functions orchestrations with compensation.
  • Holds that expire (e.g. 10-minute cart hold): Service Bus scheduled message to release unpaid holds.

Review checklist

  • Estimate shows low QPS → correctness is the focus.
  • Inventory per (hotel, room type, date).
  • Idempotency key for double submit.
  • Pessimistic vs optimistic vs constraint compared; one chosen.
  • Single-transaction invariant; saga if services split.
  • Shard by hotel; cache only on the read path.
